Rules / Modernization

SK1080 Use the LINQ operator that says what the chain means

xs.Where(x => x is T).Cast<T>() is xs.OfType<T>(), which is the operator the chain was spelling out.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

OfType<T> is defined as "test each element against T and yield the ones that pass, typed" — which is exactly what a Where holding a type test followed by a Cast<T> does, written across two operators and two iterators. The long form reads as two decisions, so a reader has to hold the filter in mind while checking that the cast agrees with it; and the two can silently stop agreeing, at which point Cast<T> throws on an element the filter was supposed to have removed. It is in the modernization range rather than the performance one because the saving — one iterator object and one delegate hop per element — is the smaller half: OfType<T> names the operation, and naming it is what stops the two halves drifting apart. It is also a shape a model writes because most of its training data predates the habit of reaching for OfType.

Example

Instead of:

var names = values.Where(value => value is string).Cast<string>();
var ids = values.Where(value => value is int).Select(value => (int)value);

Write:

var names = values.OfType<string>();
var ids = values.OfType<int>();

When it does not fire

⚠ The rewrite is exact only because `OfType<T>` is `Where(x => x is T)` followed by the cast, and every guard here exists to keep the two halves literally that. The predicate must be a one-parameter lambda whose whole body is p is T — not !(p is not T), not a type test joined to anything else — and the T it tests must be the same symbol as the one the consuming Cast<T> or cast expression names. A different T on the two sides is not this shape and rewriting it would change which elements survive. ⚠ The null case is what makes the two forms agree and is worth stating: x is T is false for a null element, so no null reaches the Cast<T>, and OfType<T> filters nulls out for the same reason — the two produce the same sequence, including for a nullable reference element type where Cast<T> on its own would happily pass null through. ⚠ The Select spelling is accepted only where its lambda body is a cast expression over its own parameter, x => (T)x, and never x => x as T — as yields null for a non-T where OfType yields nothing, so on a sequence the filter did not fully clean those are different lengths. ⚠ Both calls must resolve to System.Linq.Enumerable, and the compilation's own Enumerable must declare an OfType the fix can bind to; Queryable is excluded for the reason SK4010 excludes it, that a provider is free to translate one spelling of a pipeline and not the other. ⚠ The indexed Where(Func<T, int, bool>) overload has no OfType counterpart and is refused. ⚠ A conditional access (xs?.Where(…).Cast<T>()) is not reported, because collapsing it would mean moving the member binding rather than replacing a name. ⚠ SK4010 folds Where(p) into nine consuming operators and this rule folds it into Cast/Select; the two consumer sets are disjoint by construction, so they never both fire on one span.
